edits.before: 一种解释是（作者推断），海洋营不是他第一次决定停下。行军第二天早上，雪大得看不清路，他就决定不拔营；天晴一些后探到一块好走的浮冰，午饭后又继续走。两次决定都在衡量眼前的路还能不能走下去。扎营等待也不是新想法：在海洋营之前，他已经写下过在最近的厚浮冰上扎营、等浮冰外漂到开阔水面的方案，并说这样还能减少冰面在脚下开裂的危险。他写道，在他们的“第一个营地”，冰面曾一夜裂开两次；这段记述没有交代那是哪个营地，不能直接等同于前文所记的行军第一夜。但他确信应当先尝试行军，还特别提到这个问题有心理层面的考虑：让大家觉得自己正在朝陆地走，比坐等漂流要好。海洋营是在四天苦干之后回到这个先前暂且搁置、留作退路的方案。营地选在更结实的浮冰上，理由里挂着一个具体的指望：附近可能开出水道，那时可以划船去找陆地。等条件更有利，再做第二次尝试。

edits.before: One reading, and it is the author's, is that Ocean Camp was not the first time he chose to stop. On the march's second morning, with snow too thick to see a path, he decided not to strike camp; when it cleared and a good floe turned up, they moved on after lunch. Both decisions turned on whether the way ahead could be made. Nor was camping to wait a new idea. Before Ocean Camp he had already written down the option of camping on the nearest heavy floe and awaiting the outward drift of the pack to open water, noting that it would also lessen the peril of the ice splitting under them. He wrote that at their "first camp" the ice had split twice in one night; the passage does not say which camp that was, and it should not simply be equated with the march's first night described earlier. But he felt sure it was right to attempt a march first, noting that there was a psychological aspect too: the men would be better off feeling they were on their way to land than simply sitting and waiting for the drift. Ocean Camp, after four days of hard effort, was a return to that option he had set aside. The camp went onto a more solid floe, and the reasoning carried a specific hope: leads opening nearby, boats in the water, land to the north-west. A second attempt was to follow once conditions improved.

edits.before: 另一种解释是关于取舍的标准（作者推断）：金币被扔掉、照片被留下，他其实写了理由。他说自己对每人两磅的限额本就有些舍不得，因为极想把重量压到最低，但有些个人物品确实可以算作不可或缺：旅程可能很长，到另一头还可能要在荒凉的海岸上临时越冬，人在这种处境下需要有东西占住思绪，需要一件能想起远在海外的家乡和亲人的实物。扉页则被他撕了下来，这段记述没有写它的去向。作者的理解是：那道上限筛的不只是重量；在冰上，金币换不来什么，照片却能让人想起家。

edits.before: A second reading, and it is the author's, concerns the standard behind the choices. The sovereigns were thrown away and the photographs were kept, and he did give his reasons. He admits he rather grudged the two-pound allowance per man, so anxious was he to keep weights down, but some personal belongings could fairly be regarded as indispensable: the journey might be a long one, and there might be a winter in improvised quarters on an inhospitable coast at the other end. In his words, "A man under such conditions needs something to occupy his thoughts, some tangible memento of his home and people beyond the seas." The fly-leaf was torn out, and the passage does not say what became of it. The author's understanding is that the limit screened for more than weight: on the ice the gold coins could buy nothing, while the photographs could bring home to mind.

edits.before: Then there are alternatives the author raises for the sake of argument; nothing suggests Shackleton weighed them himself. The party could have been split in two, one half keeping up a minimal reconnaissance while the other held the camp and conserved its strength. Or a few men might have gone ahead lightly loaded, to feel out the leads. Both would have meant splitting the party. They are listed here only to show that the decision of that day was not the only possibility, though it did match the conditions in front of them.

The party could have been split in two, one half keeping up a minimal reconnaissance while the other held the camp and conserved its strength. Or a few men might have gone ahead lightly loaded, to feel out the leads. Both would have meant splitting the party. They are listed here only to show that the decision of that day was not the only possibility, though it did match the conditions in front of them.
